newsitem.title: USA: Dole hints at tougher line against Clinton.
newsitem.headline: Dole hints at tougher line against Clinton.

text.p: Republican Bob Dole on Sunday attacked President Bill Clinton on crime-fighting, gun control and the economy, and said if Americans wanted to cast their ballot "with pride," they should choose him on Election Day.

Campaigning in New Jersey, where a previous bus tour last week was drowned out by a tropical storm, Dole to generally sparce crowds pressed the same themes of trust and honesty he has since the presidential debate one week ago.

Again avoiding a direct assault on Clinton's ethics or character, he teased the audiences at his rallies about whether he should get tougher on Clinton, as some of his advisers have urged, asking: "Should I get tougher on Clinton? You won't get mad at me if I get a little tougher?"

Dole has portrayed himself as a plain-speaking, reliable man of his word, and tried to depict Clinton as a glib promise breaker who exaggerates his achievements and distorts Dole's programmes to frighten the elderly and veterans.
"Ronald Reagan used to say every day is 4th of July," he said. "Bill Clinton thinks every day is Halloween."
"I want you to be proud of the vote you cast," Dole said. "I want you to take a look at Bob Dole. Take a look at Bill Clinton. And take a look at whether we keep our word."
"Cast your vote with pride," he said.
Dole accused Clinton of taking credit for a drop in crime, when the credit properly belongs to local officials, and of exaggerating the impact of a law that would put 100,000 police on the streets.
"You won't live long enough to see 100,000 police... It ain't gonna happen," Dole said.

Dole, who opposes the Brady Bill gun control measure that Clinton signed into law in 1993, also attacked Clinton on gun control, saying: "He wouldn't take effective measures to keep guns out of the hands of criminals."

Although Dole attacked Clinton's policies across the board, he dwelt especially on his own pledge to cut taxes, the same promise that brought Gov. Christie Todd Whitman to power here in an upset victory three years ago.

"My biggest fear is that if he gets re-eleected to another four years, you better hold on to your wallets and everything that isn't nailed down, because he's coming at you," said Dole, whose central campaign message is a promised 15 percent across the board tax cut.
"Keep in mind, the typical American family spends more on taxes than they they do on food, clothing and shelter combined -- about 40 percent," he added.

Dole acknowledged that he is the underdog, but insisted that he could still turn the race around, although the size of the crowds, and the number of "thumbs down" signals he encountered along the New Jersey roads indicated he has an uphill fight.

In Newark, the state's largest city, Dole told a largely Italian-American crowd at a Columbus Day Parade that "It's not over til it's over," quoting baseball legend Yogi Berra, a long-time New Jersey resident.
A state of swing voters, New Jersey has 15 electoral votes, a popular Republican governor, and a history of voting for Republicans for president -- although it backed Clinton in 1992.
Some of Dole's aides and allies, including House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich, have ratcheted up their attacks on Clinton, using language far harsher than Dole himself has chosen.

Dole himself has walked a fine line between raising questions about Clinton's reliability and trustworthiness while not getting into Clinton's private life or dwelling too much on the Whitewater scandal.
